facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The monks, to the number of several thousands, are men of the highest ability and talent.
facts.source_name: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions
facts.text: Xuanzang's seventh-century travelogue records that Nalanda Mahavihara accommodated thousands of resident monks and visiting scholars studying Buddhist doctrines, logic, grammar, and astronomy.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Traditional Tibetan sources mention the existence of a great library at Nalanda named Dharmaganja (Piety Mart) which comprised three large multi-storeyed buildings, the Ratnasagara (Ocean of Jewels), the Ratnodadhi (Sea of Jewels), and the Ratnaranjaka (Jewel-adorned).
facts.source_name: Sum-pa mkhan-po, Pag Sam Jon Zang
facts.text: The eighteenth-century Tibetan chronicle Pag Sam Jon Zang records that Nalanda's library quarter was named Dharmaganja and consisted of three grand multi-storey edifices named Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi, and Ratnaranjaka.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Ratnodadhi was nine storeys high and housed the most sacred manuscripts including the Prajnyaparamita Sutra and the Guhyasamaja.
facts.source_name: Sum-pa mkhan-po, Pag Sam Jon Zang
facts.text: According to the Tibetan text Pag Sam Jon Zang, the library building named Ratnodadhi rose to an elevation of nine storeys and preserved rare Buddhist sutras including the Prajnaparamita and Guhyasamaja.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The exact number of volumes in the Nalanda library is not known, but it is estimated to have been in the hundreds of thousands.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / Historical consensus
facts.text: While popular tradition claims Nalanda housed 9 million manuscripts that burnt uninterrupted for three months, historians note that early medieval chronicles mention neither a specific book tally nor a three-month burn time.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: There were a great number of books on the religion of the Hindus there; and when all these books came under the observation of the Musalmans, they summoned a number of Hindus that they might give them information respecting the import of those books; but all the Hindus had been slain.
facts.text: Persian historian Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani recorded in the Tabaqat-i Nasiri that troops under Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji seized a fortified monastery in Bihar containing an extensive collection of books whose readers had perished.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: A passage from Minhaj-i-Siraj's Tabaqat-i Nasiri which actually describes the destruction of Odantapura Vihar (var. Bihar Sharif) is often taken as evidence of Nalanda's demise.
facts.text: Historians debate whether the fortress of Bihar described in the Tabaqat-i Nasiri refers to Nalanda Mahavihara or the fortified monastery complex of Odantapuri located nearby at modern Bihar Sharif.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: At Nalanda, there were 80 small viharas, which had been abandoned after being damaged by the Turushkas, and only two of the viharas were functional. Less than hundred monks resided there, and a local king named Buddhasena financially supported the Nalanda's 90-year abbot Rahula Shribhadra.
facts.text: The biography of Tibetan monk Dharmasvamin records that when he reached Nalanda around 1234 CE, roughly seventy monks still lived in surviving viharas under the guidance of the elderly master Rahula Shribhadra.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: excavations commenced in 1915, which unearthed eleven monasteries and six brick temples neatly arranged on grounds 12 hectares (30 acres) in area.
facts.text: Systematic excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India initiated in 1915 cleared eleven interconnected brick monasteries and six temples spanning a 12-hectare protected zone.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Archeological excavations at the site during 1920-1921 revealed a thick layer of ashes on the uppermost strata, across many buildings separated by some distance; this suggests that Nalanda was subject to a catastrophic fire.
facts.text: Archaeological excavations conducted across the uppermost levels of several separated monasteries in 1920 and 1921 revealed continuous layers of ash, burnt plaster, and charred wooden beams.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Legend says its library smouldered for three months.
facts.text: A popular regional legend holds that smoke and soot from the burning Dharmaganja library darkened the skies over the Magadha plains for three full months.
